system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2135-09-10 22:52:00 to 2135-09-11 16:38:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old male with a history of multiple strokes, tracheostomy, GJ tube, atrial fibrillation, and recent UTI was admitted for fever and blood from his G-tube, initially brought in for routine replacement. Imaging showed no abdominal leak, but chest findings revealed bilateral lower lobe infiltrates concerning for hospital-associated pneumonia. He was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, and a mini-BAL identified Serratia marcescens and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Antibiotics were narrowed to levofloxacin, which he continued via G-tube. The G-tube was successfully replaced without complications. His white count improved, fever resolved, and he remained stable. C. diff was ruled out despite history. His atrial fibrillation was managed with warfarin, temporarily supported with heparin until therapeutic INR was achieved. A stage 2 sacral pressure ulcer was monitored with wound care. He was discharged to extended care on oral levofloxacin for a full 14-day course and with warfarin dose increased to 4mg daily, to be titrated by rehab based on INR.
problems: Infection and inflammatory reaction due to indwelling urinary catheter
Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food or vomitus

radiology_notes.text:
PROCEDURE: Replacement of 14 ___ ___ gastrojejunal feeding tube. 
  
HISTORY: ___ year old man with CVAs and long standing GJ tube that fell out. 
  
ANESTHESIA: 10 mL of viscous lidocaine was administered around the 
gastrostomy tract. No intravenous sedation or injected lidocaine was 
required.

benefits of the procedure involved. Following this, the patient was brought to
the angiography suite and placed supine on the imaging table. The upper
abdomen was prepped and draped in the usual sterile 
fashion. A preprocedure huddle and timeout were performed as per ___ 
protocol. 
  
A scout fluoroscopic image did not show residual catheter. ___ ___  catheter

confirmed the tip of the catheter to lie in the stoamch. the catheter was

note, patient has partial malrotation with midline locations of ligament of
Treitz.  Over the ___ wire, a new 14 ___ ___ gastrojejunal feeding
tube was advanced. The pigtail formed within the duodenum, in a post-pyloric
position. The patient tolerated the procedure well. There were no early
complications. The catheter was secured with a Stat lock and sterile dressings
were applied.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand your GJ tube came out at the nursing home. We’re going to keep you here overnight to make sure everything’s stable before replacing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… tube out. Hurts leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you mentioned leg pain. We checked your vitals and labs, and you don’t have a fever or signs of infection. Your blood work shows your white count is a bit high, but we don’t see a clear source yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. Just leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your leg. The swelling might be from lying on one side. We’ll also check your INR since you’re on warfarin for your atrial fibrillation. It was 1.9 on admission—slightly low, but we’re continuing your usual dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Warfarin okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping it the same for now. Your diabetes and thyroid meds are also continuing as usual. We’re giving you pain medicine through the tube site if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re scheduling the GJ tube replacement today. An interventional radiologist will do it using imaging to guide the new tube into place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll use numbing medicine around the site. You shouldn’t feel much. You’ll be awake but won’t need sedation. The procedure usually goes smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The team just replaced your GJ tube. It went well—no complications. The tube is in the right spot and can be used for feeding right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Leg still swollen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. Your right leg and arm are both swollen. Since you have a history of clots, we recommend an ultrasound to check for a DVT. It might just be from positioning, but we want to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll arrange it soon. For now, your breathing is stable, lungs are clear, and your sacral ulcer looks clean. No signs of infection at the GJ site either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound is pending, but we’re planning to discharge you today to extended care. Your GJ tube is working, and you’re stable otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Medicines same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your medications continue as before. The rehab team will manage your warfarin and check your INR regularly to keep it in range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. Please watch for redness, swelling, or drainage at the GJ site. And the rehab team will follow up on the leg swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. You did well. The feeding tube is secure, and we’ll make sure your care continues smoothly at the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge orders are ready. You’ll go back on your regular schedule of tube feeds, medications, and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back to routine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Same meds, same feeds. Just make sure the rehab team checks your leg and your INR as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have the transport team get you ready. You should be at the facility by late afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Let the rehab team know if anything changes—especially with the leg or the tube site.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old male with a history of multiple strokes, tracheostomy, GJ tube, atrial fibrillation, and diabetes was admitted after pulling out his GJ tube at the nursing home. He was monitored overnight and found to have mild leukocytosis without an identifiable source and reported leg pain. The GJ tube was successfully replaced by interventional radiology without complications. His atrial fibrillation was managed with continued warfarin, and his INR was monitored. A stage 2 sacral ulcer was noted but remained stable. He developed new edema in the right lower and upper extremities, prompting a recommendation for DVT ultrasound. He remained stable throughout the admission and was discharged to extended care with all medications continued as before.
